name: Aisha Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Aisha, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I'm the carpentry lead for Harlow Construction, a mid-sized contractor, and we do extensions to schools and the hospital here. Right now it's six new classrooms at Greenfield Primary, so I'm setting out door frames, fitting acoustic ceilings and building cloakroom benches at child height. At weekends I run my own little business, Chen Home Repairs, fixing doors, decking and kitchen cupboards, and I found most of those customers through a website I built with an AI tool one rainy Sunday. I love finishing a classroom and knowing thirty kids will sit in it next September. What wears me out is the security checks on school sites, forty minutes some mornings just to get through the gate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you manage both, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use the AI for everything, quotes, invoices, booking customers, even planning which jobs to do on which Saturday so I'm not driving back and forth. My husband Wei is a chef at a restaurant in town, our son's married and our daughter's finishing nursing college. Money's thin because I put my savings into a second van and tools for the weekend business last year, and Harlow pays less than the city firms. I'd say two weeks in the bank, maybe three. It's a bet on myself, and I believe in betting on yourself rather than waiting for somebody to help you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great little helper, and anyone who isn't using it is missing out. I'd probably post a video of how I quote a decking job with it in five minutes. Some of the lads at Harlow would roll their eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my edge and keep growing the weekend business. It's still mostly my hands that earn the money, the AI just takes the paperwork off me. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing both. Grow Chen Home Repairs to maybe two Saturdays and a Sunday a month, pay off the van in about eighteen months, and then start saving properly. I'd take on a school-leaver on Saturdays if the work's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, actually. It's the picture where I win slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking on a school-leaver. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody took me on. Mr Okafor, the joiner I apprenticed with, let me sweep his shop and then taught me everything. You don't get given things in this life, but you can be given a chance, and that's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wei works long hours too. When do you see each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Monday nights, when the restaurant's shut. We cook together, he cooks and I wash up, and we don't talk about work. It's the best night of the week.

S0.say: She'd call AI a great little helper and say anyone not using it is missing out, posting a video of quoting a decking job in five minutes, to some eye-rolling at work.
S0.think: Privately she keeps her edge and grows her weekend business, since her hands still earn the money and AI just handles the paperwork.
S0.do: Keeps both jobs and grows her weekend repair business, paying off the second van in about eighteen months before saving properly. Considers taking on a school-leaver on Saturdays.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, the picture where she wins slowly.
S0.quote: You don't get given things in this life, but you can be given a chance, and that's different.
S0.fieldNote: She's an enthusiastic daily AI user who runs a weekend business on top of a full-time job. Her thin savings are a deliberate bet on her own business. She values being given a chance over being given help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people who get on with it. The ones who learn will do fine. I'd say that at work and online, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd do better than fine. I already use the tools every day, I've got a business on the side, and I'm the one Harlow asks when the tablet stops working. The risk is small jobs like mine get cheaper and more people start doing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Harlow to put me on the first job that uses the new setting-out robots, and I'd learn them inside out. I'd use more AI for the weekend business, get it to handle bookings by itself. And I'd look at whether one of those small robot tools, like an automatic sander, would let me do more jobs on a Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said more people would start doing small jobs. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but that's competition, and competition is fair. I'd compete on being reliable. Half my customers came to me because the last man didn't turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the people at Harlow who don't use the tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them if they asked. I'd show anyone. But I can't make them learn, and I don't think the government should pay them to sit at home instead. Brian, our site joiner, told me he'll retire before he touches a tablet, and that's his choice.

S1.say: She'd call it an opportunity for people who get on with it, saying those who learn will do fine, at work and online.
S1.think: Privately she expects to do better than fine as a daily AI user with a side business, though small jobs like hers may get cheaper as more people do them.
S1.do: Asks to be on the first job using setting-out robots and learns them thoroughly, and lets AI handle bookings for her weekend business. Looks at small robot tools, like an automatic sander, to fit more jobs into a Saturday.
S1.quote: I'd compete on being reliable. Half my customers came to me because the last man didn't turn up.
S1.fieldNote: She welcomes competition and plans to win on reliability. She'll help colleagues who ask but opposes paying people to stay home, in line with her free-market views. She sees steady change mostly as opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get moving, fast. Don't wait for the government. I'd be posting about how I'm adapting, and I'd tell anyone who'd listen that small businesses need cheap loans to get the robots, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is very fast, and I've got almost nothing saved. If robots can do any job, my weekend business is doing the same as everyone else's robots, so my edge is gone too. I'd be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look straight away at whether I could get a robot of my own on lease and turn Chen Home Repairs into a robot-assisted repair firm, with me doing the customer side. I'd sell the second van to free up money. I'd ask Harlow to keep me on supervising the robots on site for as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited and terrified at once, like the first day I ran my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two years of warning buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's enough to jump first, be the first robot repair firm in town. It's not enough to save anything, so if it goes wrong, it really goes wrong. I'd be betting on myself again, and this time it's the whole house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be doing the customer side. Why would customers want you, if the robot does the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people want somebody to trust in their home. An old lady doesn't want a machine in her kitchen with nobody to ask. She wants me, Aisha, who fixed her back door last year, standing there saying it's all right.

S2.say: She'd urge people to move fast without waiting for the government, post about how she's adapting, and argue small businesses need cheap loans for robots, not handouts.
S2.think: Privately two years is very fast and she has almost nothing saved; if robots can do any job, her weekend business loses its edge too.
S2.do: Looks at leasing a robot to turn her repair business into a robot-assisted firm, with her handling customers, and sells the second van to free up money. Asks her employer to keep her supervising site robots as long as possible.
S2.feel: Anxious, excited and terrified at once, like her first day running her own job.
S2.quote: I'd be betting on myself again, and this time it's the whole house.
S2.fieldNote: Her instinct is to jump first, but she sees that full AGI erodes even her edge, and thin savings make the bet risky. She believes trust is what customers will pay a person for. Her politics favour loans for small businesses over support payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of time for people who want to adapt. Learn, plan, and get ready. Small firms should be helped to get the machines too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a decent shape for me. Sixty-three when it arrives, and I'd have time to build up the business and some savings first. I'd feel I had a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, pay off the van and start saving. Year two, learn the robots properly at Harlow and lease one small robot for the weekend business. Year three, decide whether to go full-time on my own, with a robot or two and a school-leaver to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest difference between two years and five, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not having to bet the house. With five years I can save first and then jump. With two, I'm jumping with nothing under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Training a school-leaver, even with robots coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Somebody has to learn to run the robots and talk to the customers, and young people need someone to give them that chance. That's how it's always worked.

S3.say: She'd say five years is plenty for people who want to adapt, and that small firms should be helped to get machines too.
S3.think: Privately it's a decent shape: 63 when it arrives, with time to build the business and some savings first, so she feels she has a real chance.
S3.do: Pays off the van and starts saving in year one, learns the robots at work and leases one small robot for her weekend business in year two. Decides in year three whether to go full-time on her own with a school-leaver to train.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: With five years I can save first and then jump. With two, I'm jumping with nothing under me.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time means she doesn't have to bet everything. She still wants to train a young person, consistent with how she was given her own chance. Her plan is step by step and ambitious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a wonderful head start for anyone willing to work. Get learning. I'd make videos on how I'm doing it, for anyone who wants them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's time to build Chen Home Repairs into a proper firm and hand it to my daughter or a young apprentice before I stop. I'd be sixty-eight, and I could finish with something to pass on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the van, save, and grow the weekend business step by step. By year four or five, I'd go full-time on my own with robots doing the heavy work. I'd train a school-leaver, and maybe talk my daughter into running the bookings alongside her nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite hopeful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, she loves nursing. But I can ask. If not, the school-leaver gets it, and that's fine too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My health. If my back goes, we've got nothing saved and the business would be just me. And Wei's restaurant, if robots cook too, he'd be the one in trouble.

S4.say: She'd call ten years a wonderful head start for anyone willing to work, and offer videos on how she's adapting.
S4.think: Privately it's time to build her repair business into a proper firm and hand it to her daughter or an apprentice before she stops at 68.
S4.do: Pays off the van, saves and grows the weekend business step by step, going full-time on her own with robots doing heavy work by year four or five. Trains a school-leaver and asks her daughter about handling bookings.
S4.quote: If not, the school-leaver gets it, and that's fine too.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets her build something to pass on. Thin savings mean her health is the main remaining risk. She also worries about her husband's job as a chef, which she hadn't mentioned before.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I can't adapt, but because I'd have nothing under me when I jump. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to lease the robots, and keeping apprenticeships going, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. People think it's all about who can do the work cheapest. But people let me into their homes because they trust me, and I don't think a machine gets that for a long time.

headlineQuote: She wants me, Aisha, who fixed her back door last year, standing there saying it's all right.
portrait: Aisha Chen is a 58-year-old carpentry lead on school and hospital extensions who runs a weekend repair business she found customers for with a website built by AI. She put her savings into a second van, a bet on herself that leaves only two or three weeks in the bank, and she believes in chances over handouts. She is calm in a plateau and in steady change, which she sees as opportunity. AGI in two years makes her anxious because she'd jump with nothing under her, but with five or ten years she plans to save first and build a robot-assisted repair firm to pass on.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have nothing saved under her when she made the jump.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small firms to lease the robots and keeping apprenticeships going, rather than handouts.
